question_text: Who is the named service owner accountable for service outcomes — not just IT processes — and when did they last make a documented decision about service priorities or improvement investment?
hidden_risk: Service ownership is nominally assigned but not exercised. No one is truly accountable when the service underperforms. Ownership is a title, not a responsibility.
select_options: ["There is no named service owner. Accountability is diffused across multiple people or teams.","A name exists on a chart but the person is not actively accountable for service outcomes.","A named owner exists and attends reviews, but cannot demonstrate recent decisions or interventions.","Named owner, actively engaged, with evidence of decisions made in the last quarter.","Named owner, fully accountable, evidence of regular decisions on priorities and investment in the last quarter."]

question_text: If an incoming IT director reviewed the service catalogue and operating documentation today, would they find a current, accurate picture of what the service delivers — or an historical document that no longer reflects operational reality?
hidden_risk: The catalogue describes what was built at implementation, not what is operated today. New services have been added informally. Retired services are still listed. Customers are requesting services that no longer exist.
score_anchors: ["The catalogue is out of date by more than 12 months and does not reflect the current service.","Significantly out of date. Multiple services added or retired without the catalogue being updated.","Partially current. The main services are reflected but gaps and inaccuracies are known.","Mostly current with minor gaps. Reviewed in the last 6-12 months.","Fully current. Reviewed within 6 months. Used operationally by the service desk."]

question_text: Is P1/P2 incident volume trending up, down, or flat over the last quarter — and has the most recent P1 post-incident review been completed with all actions formally tracked to closure?
hidden_risk: Incident volume is rising but the trend is not being tracked. Post-incident reviews are written but not actioned. The same failure modes recur because learning is not embedded.
select_options: ["Volume is rising and there is no post-incident review process. Nothing is being learnt.","Volume is flat or rising. Post-incident reviews are written but actions are not tracked to closure.","Volume is broadly flat. Reviews are written but action completion is inconsistent.","Volume is stable or declining. Most PIR actions are tracked and closed.","Volume is declining. Every P1 PIR is completed. All actions are closed or in tracked remediation with evidence."]

question_text: How confident are you that a significant service incident occurring tomorrow would be detected by your monitoring tools before users report it — and would be resolved within your defined targets?
hidden_risk: The service learns about incidents from user complaints rather than proactive monitoring. Response is reactive by design. Monitoring tools generate noise that is largely ignored.
score_anchors: ["The service learns about incidents from user complaints. Monitoring tools are not trusted or not in place.","Monitoring exists but alert volumes are unmanaged. Most alerts are ignored.","Monitoring detects some incidents proactively but coverage and alert quality are inconsistent.","Monitoring detects the majority of incidents before users report them. Resolution targets are broadly met.","Proactive detection evidenced. Alert quality is managed. Resolution within defined targets consistently achieved."]

question_text: To what extent are service requests formally separated from incidents in the tooling — with fulfilment times tracked, reported, and consistently meeting defined targets?
hidden_risk: Requests and incidents are mixed. Neither is being managed correctly. SLA reporting is unreliable. Customers cannot distinguish between a request and an incident.
score_anchors: ["Requests and incidents are mixed in the same queue. Neither is being managed correctly.","Broadly separated but processes are not distinct and targets are not defined.","Separated in tooling but fulfilment targets are inconsistently met.","Clear separation. Targets defined and mostly met. Reviewed monthly.","Full separation. Distinct processes and SLAs. Targets consistently met. Evidence available."]

question_text: When a standard service request arrives, is there a documented process that every agent follows regardless of who receives it — or does fulfilment depend on individual knowledge and experience?
hidden_risk: Request handling varies by individual. Customers receive inconsistent service. Fulfilment times vary by agent, not by request complexity.
select_options: ["No documented processes exist. Fulfilment depends entirely on individual knowledge and experience.","Processes exist for some request types but most are handled by individual judgement.","Processes are documented but inconsistently followed. Quality varies by agent.","Documented processes for all standard requests. Followed consistently by most agents.","All standard requests follow documented processes. Quality is monitored. Evidence of consistent application."]

question_text: How many problems were formally opened and closed in the last 30 days — and what is the oldest open item in the Known Error Database with its documented reason for remaining unresolved?
hidden_risk: The organisation claims to have problem management but records are created without action. The same known errors persist indefinitely. Root causes are never permanently resolved.
select_options: ["No active problem management. The KEDB is not maintained or does not exist.","Some problem records exist but are not actively managed. The KEDB has aged items with no justification.","Problem management is active but inconsistent. Some items remain open beyond 90 days without a documented reason.","Active problem management with named owners. No items over 90 days without a documented approved deferral reason.","Rigorous problem management. Regular reviews. All items have named owners and resolution dates. Measurable reduction in repeat incidents."]

question_text: To what extent is problem management genuinely preventing recurrence — rather than existing nominally with records created but actions never completed?
hidden_risk: Problem management is a process on paper. Problems are opened, a root cause is documented, and nothing changes. The same incidents recur week after week.
score_anchors: ["Problem management is nominal. Records are created but no recurrence reduction is evidenced.","Some problems resolved but the process is inconsistent and improvement is not measurable.","Problems are resolved but tracking to recurrence reduction is not consistent.","Measurable reduction in repeat incidents in most areas. Process consistently applied.","Clear evidenced reduction in repeat incidents attributable to problem resolution. Process fully embedded."]

question_text: What is the change failure rate over the last quarter — and does the incident data confirm that failed changes are not a regular source of service incidents?
hidden_risk: Failed changes are causing incidents that are then managed as BAU. The change and incident functions are masking each other. The real cause of service instability is uncontrolled change.
select_options: ["Failure rate above 15% or changes are regularly causing incidents. No root cause analysis conducted.","Elevated failure rate. Changes are occasionally causing incidents. Limited root cause work.","Failure rate is tracked but improvement is not consistent. Some change-related incidents remain.","Failure rate is below 10% and declining. Change-related incidents are rare.","Failure rate below 5% and declining. Root cause analysis on every failure. Incident correlation confirmed."]

question_text: What percentage of changes in the last quarter were emergency changes — and does this reflect genuine operational urgency or a pattern of bypassing the standard change process?
hidden_risk: Emergency change is being used as a workaround for a weak standard change process. The CAB is being bypassed routinely. Controls exist on paper but not in practice.
select_options: ["Emergency changes above 20% of volume. The standard process is being routinely bypassed.","Elevated at 10-20%. Emergency change is used regularly to avoid the standard CAB process.","Borderline at 5-10%. Some emergency changes are not fully justified as genuine emergencies.","Below 5%. Each emergency change is formally justified. Standard process is the norm.","Below 5% and declining. Every emergency change is formally reviewed post-implementation."]

question_text: Have any SLA targets been revised downward in the last 12 months — and do the current targets represent genuine service expectations or levels set to avoid breach reporting?
hidden_risk: SLA gaming: targets have been reduced to the level the service can actually achieve. Compliance is maintained by lowering the bar, not improving the service.
select_options: ["Targets have been revised downward to avoid breach. Compliance is maintained by lowering the bar.","Targets have been adjusted more than once. The direction of change is always downward.","Targets have not changed but the business regularly challenges whether they reflect actual expectations.","Targets are challenging and unchanged. Occasional misses are addressed through improvement not target reduction.","Targets are challenging, unchanged, consistently met, and validated by business satisfaction data."]

question_text: How confident are you that service reporting drives decisions and improvement actions — rather than being produced for compliance and filed without discussion?
hidden_risk: Reports are produced but nobody acts on them. The data is collected but intelligence is not extracted. Reporting is a governance exercise, not a management tool.
score_anchors: ["Reports are produced but nobody reviews or acts on them.","Reports are reviewed occasionally but rarely produce specific actions.","Reports are reviewed regularly but actions are inconsistent and not always followed through.","Reports consistently drive service review discussions and produce documented actions.","Reports are the foundation of service management. Every review produces documented decisions and tracked improvement actions."]

question_text: When the last significant new or changed service was handed over to BAU, was there a formal acceptance process — with completed documentation, training, and confirmed operational readiness before handover?
hidden_risk: Projects hand over to BAU without formal acceptance. Operations receive systems they were not involved in building. Transition produces immediate operational instability.
select_options: ["No formal transition process. Services are handed over when the project team decides they are ready.","A process exists informally but it was not formally followed for the last transition.","A process was followed but documentation was incomplete and readiness was not formally confirmed.","Formal acceptance process followed. Documentation mostly completed. Operational readiness confirmed.","Full formal acceptance process. All documentation completed. Operational readiness independently confirmed with evidence."]

question_text: To what extent does the organisation have a formally defined New Service Introduction process — covering readiness assessment, transition criteria, hypercare activation, and the conditions for formal BAU acceptance?
hidden_risk: Every new or changed service is introduced differently depending on who is managing it. There is no institutional process. Transition quality depends entirely on individual judgement.
score_anchors: ["No formal NSI process exists. Every new service is introduced differently.","An informal approach exists but it is not documented or consistently applied.","A process is partially documented but not consistently followed across all service introductions.","Formal NSI process documented and applied to most significant service introductions.","Formal NSI process documented, mandatory, consistently followed, evidence of application available."]

question_text: What is the current first-contact resolution rate at the service desk — is it tracked, and is it meeting its defined target?
hidden_risk: The service desk is firefighting. FCR is unknown. Customers are following up on unresolved requests through informal channels because the official process is not working.
select_options: ["FCR is not tracked. The service desk primarily logs tickets and escalates.","FCR is tracked but below 50%. The service desk has limited resolution capability.","FCR is tracked but below target. Improvement actions exist but progress is slow.","FCR is at or approaching its target. Improvement is active and measurable.","FCR is at or above target. Monitored monthly. Driving coaching and knowledge base improvements."]

question_text: What would happen if ticket volume increased by 30% tomorrow — does the service have a formal capacity plan and a tested process for scaling support when demand exceeds current resource?
hidden_risk: The service is operating at or near capacity. The next growth event will cause degradation. Nobody is planning for it. Leadership will be surprised.
score_anchors: ["No capacity plan exists. A volume increase would cause immediate degradation with no response plan.","Capacity is managed reactively. There is no formal plan or defined scaling process.","Capacity is informally managed. Some awareness of thresholds but no formal plan.","A capacity plan exists. Scaling thresholds are defined. A response process is documented.","Formal capacity plan. Scaling thresholds defined and tested. Leadership has full visibility of the plan."]

question_text: Are vendor SLAs formally tracked and reported — and is there current, documented evidence to support any commercial challenge if a vendor is not meeting its contractual commitments?
hidden_risk: The organisation believes vendors are underperforming but has no data to challenge the contract. Relationships are managed informally. Commercial leverage is lost.
select_options: ["No formal vendor SLA tracking. Vendor performance is managed by conversation not data.","Some tracking exists but the data is not structured enough to support a commercial challenge.","Tracking is in place but has not been used in a commercial conversation.","Monthly vendor reviews with contractual performance data. Has been used to raise formal concerns.","Formal monthly reviews with documented evidence. Used to challenge and improve vendor performance."]

question_text: To what extent is accountability clearly defined at every vendor boundary — with a RACI that confirms who owns what for every service component, leaving no gaps at the interface between internal teams and external providers?
hidden_risk: Vendor and internal team boundaries are unclear. When something fails, neither party accepts ownership. The customer suffers while responsibility is disputed.
score_anchors: ["Known accountability gaps exist at vendor boundaries. Disputes about ownership are common.","Broadly defined but significant gaps remain in edge cases and interface areas.","Generally defined but gaps exist at some vendor boundaries.","RACI defined for all main service components. Validated with vendors.","RACI defined for all service components. Validated with vendors. Embedded in contracts."]

question_text: When was the last full DR test conducted — and did the organisation meet its defined RTO and RPO targets, with all findings formally actioned?
hidden_risk: DR exists on paper but has never been proven under realistic conditions. The organisation does not know whether it can recover within its defined targets.
select_options: ["No DR test has been conducted in the last 12 months, or no test has ever been conducted.","A test was conducted but RTO and RPO targets were not met.","A test was conducted and targets were broadly met, but not all findings have been actioned.","Annual test completed. Targets met. Most findings actioned.","Annual test completed. Targets met. All findings formally actioned with evidence before the next test."]

question_text: To what extent are all known single points of failure formally mitigated or accepted at board level — with documented workarounds for any that remain unresolved?
hidden_risk: Known SPOFs are accepted because remediation has been deferred. A single failure will cause a significant outage and the organisation has no workaround.
score_anchors: ["Known SPOFs exist with no mitigation plan. A single failure would cause a significant unrecoverable outage.","SPOFs are known but mitigation has been deferred with no formal acceptance or workaround.","SPOFs are documented. Mitigation is incomplete. Some have accepted workarounds, others do not.","Most SPOFs formally mitigated. Remaining items are board-accepted with documented workarounds.","All known SPOFs formally mitigated or accepted at board level. Workarounds documented for all accepted items."]

pillar_code: DD11 — Service Tooling, CMDB & Knowledge Management
question_text: What percentage of the top five highest-volume ticket types are handled through automation or self-service — and when was the knowledge base last formally reviewed for accuracy and currency?
hidden_risk: Agents handle the same routine requests manually every day. The knowledge base was built during implementation and has not been maintained. Automation exists in the roadmap but not in operations.
select_options: ["No automation for high-volume types. The knowledge base was built at implementation and has not been maintained.","Minimal automation. The knowledge base exists but is significantly out of date.","Partial automation for some ticket types. Knowledge base is partially current.","Top 3 or more volume types automated. Knowledge base reviewed within the last 12 months.","Top 5 volume types automated with measurable FCR improvement. Knowledge base reviewed within 6 months."]

pillar_code: DD11 — Service Tooling, CMDB & Knowledge Management
question_text: How confident are you that the CMDB accurately reflects the current service estate — and has its accuracy been formally assessed in the last 12 months with known gaps formally accepted?
hidden_risk: The CMDB is inaccurate. Change and incident processes are making decisions based on incorrect configuration data. Impact assessments are wrong because the CMDB cannot be trusted.
score_anchors: ["The CMDB has not been reviewed in over 12 months. Its accuracy is unknown.","The CMDB is known to be inaccurate. Changes and incidents are being managed on incorrect data.","Reviewed but known gaps have not been remediated. Accuracy is below 80%.","Reviewed within 12 months. Accuracy above 80%. Maintenance process is in place.","Reviewed within 12 months. Accuracy above 90%. Maintained by a defined process with regular updates."]

question_text: Is there a named individual accountable for continuous service improvement — not just a process that exists in the framework documentation — and what improvement did they initiate in the last quarter?
hidden_risk: CSI is in the framework catalogue but no one is actually doing it. Reports are produced, improvement opportunities identified, and nothing changes.
select_options: ["No named CSI owner. No recent improvement has been initiated or delivered.","A name is associated with CSI but no improvement has been delivered in the last quarter.","A named owner exists and has initiated improvements but delivery has been inconsistent.","Named owner, actively initiating improvements, with evidence of at least one delivered in the last quarter.","Named owner, accountable, with evidence of two or more improvements initiated and delivered in the last quarter."]

question_text: To what extent does the organisation measure user satisfaction beyond ticket volume and SLA compliance — asking the business whether the service is actually meeting their needs?
hidden_risk: SLA compliance is 98% and user satisfaction is 3 out of 10. The metrics do not reflect the experience. The business is not being heard.
score_anchors: ["No user satisfaction measurement beyond SLA. The business is never formally asked.","Occasional informal feedback. Nothing structured or regular.","Some measurement exists but results are not acted upon or visible to leadership.","Regular satisfaction measurement. Results are visible to leadership and produce some improvement actions.","Regular measurement. Results visible to leadership. Documented improvement actions result from every review cycle."]
